extracted.intended_audience: writers, students, and readers interested in narrative theory and character creation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and principles for representing and developing characters in narrative and dramatic works, covering direct vs indirect methods, voice, archetypes, and drama-specific constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct (explicit) characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: The author literally tells the audience what a character is like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This may be done via the narrator, another character, or by the character themselves. Direct characterization is an explicit method of conveying qualities to the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect (implicit) characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience must infer for themselves what the character is like through the character's thoughts, actions, speech (choice of words, manner of speaking), physical appearance, mannerisms and interaction with other characters, including other characters' reactions to that particular person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also called the 'dramatic' method; invites readers to draw conclusions from behavior and dialogue rather than being told. Useful for 'showing' character rather than 'telling.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Show characters through actions and speech (differentiation)
rubrics_metrics.description: To differentiate characters in fiction, the writer must show them doing and saying things; a character must be defined by more than one single topic of conversation or by the character's accent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A character should have other interests or personality quirks in addition to any single dominant trait (e.g., accent or one topic). Showing via behavior and dialogue makes characters distinct and believable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character's voice (manner of speech) must be distinctive
rubrics_metrics.description: A character's voice is their manner of speech; different characters use different vocabularies and rhythms of speech. In theory, a reader should be able to identify which character is speaking simply from the way they talk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a character voice has been created that is rich and distinctive, the writer can get away with omitting many speech attributions (tag lines). Voice should be rich enough to allow omission of tags, but must be consistent and recognizable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue realism factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Although individual temperament is the largest determinant of what a character says, it is not the only one; consider personality psychology, age, culture, family background, region, gender, education, and circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these factors to make characters' dialogue more realistic and interesting. Tailor vocabulary, cadence, and references to the character's background and situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction and speech elements that characterize
rubrics_metrics.description: Words characterize by their diction, cadence, complexity, attitude and fluency. Mannerisms and catch-phrases can help too. Considering the degree of formality in spoken language is also useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements such as tone of voice, volume, rate of delivery, vocabulary, inflection, emphasis, pitch, topics of conversation, idioms, colloquialisms, and figures of speech all express who the character is on the inside. Use them deliberately to signal personality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice should originate from interior psychology (inside-out)
rubrics_metrics.description: A character's manner of speech must grow from the inside out; the speaking is how their essential personality leaks out for the world to see; it is not the sum total of their personality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure dialogue and utterances reflect an underlying psychology and history, rather than being merely stylistic flourishes. Avoid voices that feel pasted-on or superficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctive voice as a unifying criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Each character should have their distinctive voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinctive voice is central to character differentiation across scenes and allows readers to follow multi-character exchanges without confusion; avoid flattening multiple characters into similar speech patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama-specific constraints and affordances
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters in theater, television, and film differ from those in novels in that an actor may interpret the writer's description and dialogue in their own unique way to add new layers and depth to a character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In drama it is not possible to 'go inside the character's head' in the way possible in a novel (interior exposition is unavailable). Conversely, characters can be seen and heard and thus need not always be described; actors' performances can supply subtext and nuance (e.g., critics comparing different actors' portrayals of 'Lady Macbeth' or 'Heathcliff').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and limits of mythological archetypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Mythological characters have been depicted to be formulaic and are part of a classification that consists of several differing, limited archetypes; Carl Jung identified twelve primary 'original patterns' of the human psyche that are often cited in fictional characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jung's twelve archetypes (Innocent, Orphan, Hero, Caregiver, Explorer, Rebel, Lover, Creator, Jester, Sage, Magician, Ruler) can serve as starting templates, but their use is often reductive; writers should avoid relying on archetypes to the point of cliché and instead mix components to create fuller characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat versus complex (realistic) characters
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Flat' characters may be considered so because they stick to a single archetype without deviating, whereas 'complex' or 'realistic' characters will combine several archetypes, with some being more dominant than others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid flatness, blend archetypal elements, add contradictions and development over time. Complexity often arises from combining motives, traits, and background in non-stereotyped ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about reductive archetype usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Jung's notions of character archetypes have been considered problematic; the use of these archetypes is often reductive and unhelpful for many writers since it simplifies character complexity into clichéd tropes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When borrowing from mythology or archetypal templates, be mindful of cultural change and the risk of stereotyping; adapt archetypes thoughtfully rather than applying them raw.
